events.text: The elders of {phl4_order} gather on the terrace at dusk and lay out the creed on a long table, line by line, like a meal. It is not complicated. It asks one thing above all, and gives one thing back. They look at you the way a mountain looks at a traveller: not unkindly, but with no great hurry for the answer. A lamp burns at the end of the table. Whoever swears lights it.

choices.text: Swear the creed, and light the lamp

effects.log: The lamp catches at once. Something in your breathing settles and does not come loose again.

choices.text: Decline politely, and keep your own counsel

effects.log: The elders nod. No one is offended, and the lamp stays dark.

events.text: An old attendant of {phl4_order} brings you a cup, and in the cup, a folded slip. On the slip are seven words. They are the creed in its shortest form, the one the faction keeps for those it expects to keep it. Swearing is simple: drink. Declining is simple too: set the cup down. The attendant stands there patiently, hands folded in sleeves.

choices.text: Drink the cup

effects.log: It tastes of nothing, and then of iron, and then of a kind of calm. The slip burns in your hand.

choices.text: Set the cup down on the stone

effects.log: The attendant bows and removes it. It is the end of the matter, for now.

events.text: The creed of {phl4_order} is carved on the wall of the Hall of Vows, and every visitor reads it, and almost no one stays to be asked. You stay. An elder tells you the creed has no loopholes, that it was written by someone who had tried them all. It will give you something real, she says, and in return will take something real. The nature of both is on the wall.

choices.text: Take the vow

effects.log: You say the words aloud in the empty hall. They are heavier than they looked on the wall.

choices.text: Read the wall once more, and leave without swearing

effects.log: You read it twice, and leave. The words follow you down the stairs.

events.text: A trial of {phl4_order}, announced without warning, set at the foot of its Hall of Vows: a master of the creed stands on the stair and does not move. You may pass, or you may be turned aside. No one cares which. The creed is not served by those who are given the stair; it is served by those who earn it, and an earned stair is a heavy thing.

choices.text: Climb through the master's stance

ok.log: You climb. The master steps aside at the last step, without a word, and the stair is yours.

fail.log: You are turned aside, politely, with a bruise to mark the place. The stair remains where it was.

choices.text: Ask to be tried in another season

effects.log: The request is noted. The master says the creed is patient, and so is the stair.

events.text: In the grey hour a bell of {phl4_order} rings once, and every sworn member rises. You do too. The trial is simple: for the length of a long breath you must hold the creed in the face of someone who wishes you to drop it. The someone is a senior of the faction, calm, and entirely sincere in trying. The air between you thickens like syrup.

choices.text: Hold the creed against the senior's pressure

ok.log: You hold. At the end of the breath the senior lowers their hands and bows, and the bell rings again.

fail.log: The pressure takes you at the knees. The senior helps you up, correctly, and says you are not yet done.

choices.text: Kneel and admit you are not ready

effects.log: The senior nods slowly. There is no shame in it, and no credit either.

events.text: A test of {phl4_order} comes in the shape of a single plain door. Whatever is behind it is for you alone, the attendant says, and the creed will be there with it. You open it. The room is bare, and in the middle of it stands someone who looks a great deal like you. They are holding the creed in their hand like a blade.

choices.text: Fight your own shadow of the creed

ok.log: The shadow fights well, and fails. The room is empty when you leave, and the creed is a little lighter.

fail.log: The shadow fights better. You stagger out with your ribs aching and the creed unproven.

choices.text: Close the door and try another day

effects.log: The door closes gently. Whatever is behind it waits, as patient as the faction.

events.text: You are offered something you want very badly, and the creed of {phl4_order} says no. A rival has laid it out for you in a quiet room: a gift, a position, a door that would not otherwise open. The vow is not mentioned. Everyone in the room knows what it says. The rival waits with a cup in each hand, and lets the silence do the asking.

choices.text: Take the gift, and let the vow break

effects.log: You take it. It is a good gift. Something quiet in you goes out like a lamp.

choices.text: Set the gift aside and keep the vow

effects.log: You set it aside. The rival nods, without malice, and drinks both cups.

events.text: A situation arises, small and awkward, where the creed of {phl4_order} would cost you something real, and breaking it would cost nothing anyone could see. A friend pleads, gently. The faction is far away. The cloud below is empty. It would be the smallest of lapses, the sort the creed was written to forbid precisely because it is small.

choices.text: Break it, quietly, this once

effects.log: You do. Nobody sees, and you know. The knowledge sits in you like a stone.

choices.text: Hold to the creed, and bear the cost

effects.log: The cost is real. You pay it, and the friend turns away, and the creed sits lighter than it did.

events.text: Late one night the words of the creed of {phl4_order} come back to you, and so does a version of yourself who never swore. That version is richer, freer, and a little lonelier than you expected. It does not argue. It simply stands at the edge of the lamplight, wearing your face, and waits for you to notice you could join it.

choices.text: Step toward the other self

effects.log: You step. The creed goes thin in your hands, and you feel it go.

choices.text: Turn your back and trim the lamp

effects.log: You trim the lamp. The other self fades. The creed settles into its old shape.

events.text: A hunter of {phl4_order} finds you on a bridge between two clouds. {npc} carries no banner and needs none. The creed was given to you freely, {he} says, and it does not take back a thing it has given, but it does take back what was broken. {He} sets down a pack, unties a cord, and offers you the choice the faction always offers: to be answered, or to answer.

choices.text: Fight {npc} on the bridge

ok.log: The bridge sings and holds. {npc} steps back, bows once, and goes the way {he} came.

fail.log: The bridge gives under both of you. {npc} is the better swimmer in air, and you are left clinging to a rope.

choices.text: Atone, and take what the faction asks

effects.log: You kneel on the bridge and say it plainly. {npc} listens to all of it and does not interrupt.

events.text: The creed of {phl4_order} is a quiet thing until it is not. {npc} arrives at your door at the turn of the evening, pleasant, tired, and well-informed, and says {he} is sorry to be here. {He} was asked to come, and {he} did. If you will answer, {he} will take the answer back. If you will not, {he} will take something else.

choices.text: Refuse, and meet {npc} in the court

ok.log: The court rings. {npc} yields, at last, and gives a short, correct bow.

fail.log: The court is smaller than you remembered. {npc} wins with a kind of regret, and withdraws.

choices.text: Answer for what you did

effects.log: You answer. It takes an hour, and it is the longest hour of the year.

events.text: {npc}, a hunter of {phl4_order}, has been three days behind you on the cloud-road. Now, at an inn with no name, {he} takes the next table and orders tea. The two of you drink your tea in silence. Eventually {he} says the faction does not forget and does not forgive, but does accept. There is a way out of this, {he} adds, and a way through, and {he} will not choose for you.

choices.text: Stand, and go through

ok.log: It is a short, clean fight. {npc} concedes with grace, and leaves the tea half-drunk.

fail.log: It is a short, clean fight. {npc} leaves you on the floor, politely, with the bill paid.

choices.text: Sit, and take the way out

effects.log: You sit. {npc} writes down what you say. It will be enough, or it will not.

events.text: The last of the hunters of {phl4_order} comes to nothing. A letter is delivered by a child, sealed in the faction's grey wax, saying that the matter is closed. It does not say whether you were forgiven or only tired out. The faction's pen is dry, and so, for the first time in years, is your sleeve. You read the letter, fold it, and discover your hands are not quite steady.

choices.text: Keep the letter where you can see it

effects.log: It sits on your desk. You glance at it each morning, and each morning it weighs less.

choices.text: Burn the letter, and take a long walk

effects.log: The ash blows off the ledge. The walk takes all day.

events.text: It is over. {phl4_order} sends no more hunters, and the creed no longer sits in your ear like a bell. The faction's elders have drawn a line under you, and you feel, oddly, the lack of it. A rival acquaintance passes you on the stairs and does not look at your belt, where the knot used to be. You are, in some way, ordinary again.

choices.text: Enjoy the ordinary

effects.log: It is quieter than you thought. You sleep well, for a season.

choices.text: Look for a new creed

effects.log: You look. It is slow, and it is yours.

events.text: The priests of {phl4_order} lay the doctrine before you at the high altar, one article after another. It is a hard doctrine and a clean one. In return it offers a kind of steadiness that no god can get on their own. Swearing is the work of a moment; breaking it, the Book of Fates is careful to note, is a Transgression, and the Book does not forgive casually.

choices.text: Swear the doctrine at the altar

effects.log: The oath settles on you like a robe. The altar-flame leans toward you and stands straight.

choices.text: Decline, and honour the altar anyway

effects.log: The priests incline their heads. The flame stays where it was, indifferent and warm.

events.text: A priest of {phl4_order} comes to your temple with the doctrine written on a single leaf. It is short. It has seven clauses, and each clause is a door that closes behind you. The priest says nothing to sell it. The leaf is held out on an open palm, and the rest is yours to do. A breeze crosses the cloister and the leaf does not stir.

choices.text: Take the leaf

effects.log: It is lighter than it looks. The seven clauses settle one by one into the space behind your ribs.

choices.text: Fold the leaf back into the priest's hand

effects.log: The priest folds it carefully away. Neither of you remarks on it.

events.text: On the day of the doctrine, the high priests of {phl4_order} come down the processional way in white and read it aloud to the open air. When they reach the end they turn to you and wait. The doctrine is old. It was old when the oldest god was young. Swearing is a link in a chain that reaches a very long way back, and a very long way forward.

choices.text: Swear, and join the chain

effects.log: You say the words. The chain tightens, then settles. It is a good chain, as chains go.

choices.text: Remain outside the chain

effects.log: You step back. The priests accept it as they accept the weather.

events.text: A trial of {phl4_order}: a lesser god of the doctrine's strictest school waits at the foot of the sanctum steps, arms folded, wearing the face of someone who has done this many times and has not once been bored. The doctrine says that to hold a clause is to be tested on it. The god offers a blessing before the first blow, and a second after, whichever way it falls.

choices.text: Hold your clause against the god's strictness

ok.log: The god strikes, and you hold. At the end they give a short nod and step aside.

fail.log: The god strikes, and you give ground. The blessing after is real, and comes with a lesson.

choices.text: Ask for a gentler test in a later season

effects.log: The god considers, and says the doctrine is a patient thing.

events.text: In the hour before the offering, {phl4_order} summons you to the Hall of Prayers and sets a single clause before you, written in light. It is the hardest of the doctrine. The light bears down like water. A great weight settles on your shoulders and you are asked, kindly, to continue to stand. Behind you the other sworn gods fall silent, watching.

choices.text: Stand under the weight of the clause

ok.log: You stand. The light eases, then lifts, and the hall breathes out around you.

fail.log: The weight takes you to your knees. The priests help you rise and say nothing unkind.

choices.text: Step out from under, and rest

effects.log: You step out. The light keeps its place, unreproaching.

events.text: A trial of the doctrine is a small shrine, and in the shrine, a mirror. {phl4_order} asks only that you look. What you see is yourself as the doctrine would have you: a little taller, a little calmer, a little less like the person who walked in. The reflection raises a hand. The mirror, it seems, will not let you leave until one of you yields.

choices.text: Contest the reflection

ok.log: The reflection yields, in the end, with a nod. The mirror clears.

fail.log: The reflection holds. You leave the shrine bruised, with the mirror dim behind you.

choices.text: Look away and try another day

effects.log: You look away. The mirror clouds slowly, as if disappointed.

events.text: A rival pantheon's envoy offers you something that {phl4_order}'s doctrine forbids. It is a very good offer. The envoy has brought a cup and does not drink from it. The doctrine says no, and a Transgression in the Book of Fates would be entered the instant you said yes. The envoy knows. The envoy waits as a river waits for a stone to move.

choices.text: Accept the offer, and take the Transgression

effects.log: You accept. The Book stirs somewhere a long way off. It is a good gift. The cost is not yet known.

choices.text: Refuse, and keep the doctrine

effects.log: You refuse. The envoy drinks from the cup after all, and says the offer will not come twice.

events.text: A small matter, an awkward one: the doctrine of {phl4_order} would have you hold back mercy, and a petitioner at your altar needs it. The Book of Fates has already begun to prepare a margin. A single act would set it right and spoil the doctrine. The petitioner does not know the stakes. They only know the shape of their need.

choices.text: Show mercy, and break the doctrine

effects.log: You show it. The petitioner leaves lighter. The Book enters a short, clinical line.

choices.text: Hold the doctrine, and deny the plea

effects.log: You deny it. The petitioner leaves heavier. The doctrine is kept, and it weighs.

events.text: At the quiet hour a voice you half-trust asks why the doctrine of {phl4_order} must be obeyed to the letter. The voice has a point. It has several points. By the end of the hour you have almost been persuaded that the doctrine would be better served by breaking it. The voice withdraws, politely, leaving the case on the table for you to finish.

choices.text: Finish the case, and break the doctrine

effects.log: You finish it. It is persuasive. The Transgression is entered by morning.

choices.text: Close the case, and keep the doctrine

effects.log: You close it. The voice, wherever it went, is a little disappointed and a little proud.

events.text: {npc}, an inquisitor of {phl4_order}, finds you at a crossroads shrine, where the incense is thin and the roads divide. {He} wears the grey of the doctrine and carries no weapon you can see. The Book of Fates has your name in a margin, {he} says, in the matter of a Transgression. {He} would like to settle it here, in the open air, in whatever way you choose.

choices.text: Contest the charge against {npc}

ok.log: The crossroads rings. {npc} yields, and writes a short, careful line in a grey book.

fail.log: The contest turns against you. {npc} accepts your surrender with practised courtesy.

choices.text: Atone, and accept the doctrine's penance

effects.log: You kneel at the shrine. {npc} listens, and takes up the pen.

events.text: {phl4_order} sends a hunter to your temple, a lesser god with a voice like a closing door. {npc} sits in your Hall of Prayers and does not touch the offerings. The doctrine was broken, {he} says, and the Book has noted it. {He} has no wish to be cruel. {He} has only to ask: will you answer, or will you be answered?

choices.text: Refuse, and face {npc} in your own hall

ok.log: The hall holds the contest well. {npc} concedes, and takes the long way home.

fail.log: The contest ends against you. {npc} nods, almost sadly, and sets a seal on the door.

choices.text: Answer for the breach, in full

effects.log: You answer. {npc} writes it all down and does not once look up.

events.text: On the third night a hunter of the doctrine, {npc}, sits beside your altar and eats a quiet meal of rice and plums. {He} makes no demand. {He} is only there, {he} says, to see that the doctrine is not forgotten. If you would like to talk of how it was broken, {he} is listening. If you would like to fight, {he} has come prepared.

choices.text: Fight {npc}, since the matter is plain

ok.log: The fight is plain and swift. {npc} yields at the last, and takes the rest of the plums.

fail.log: The fight is plain and swift. {npc} yields nothing, and the plums are cold by the time you wake.

choices.text: Talk, and let {npc} listen

effects.log: You talk. {npc} listens in silence until the last plum.

events.text: The last hunter of {phl4_order} withdraws, and a leaf of the doctrine floats down onto your altar with a line struck through. The matter is closed. The Book of Fates has crossed out the Transgression, neat as a clerk. Whether this is forgiveness or fatigue, no priest can tell you. You hold the leaf up to the lamp and find that you can see right through it.

choices.text: Keep the struck leaf

effects.log: It rests in your sleeve, light as breath. It is a small thing, and it matters.

choices.text: Offer the leaf to the altar-flame

effects.log: It burns blue and goes up. The altar seems, if anything, content.

events.text: It is quiet. {phl4_order} sends no more hunters. The doctrine lies lightly on the air, and you are no longer the subject of any page. A lesser god passing on the cloister steps nods to you, and the nod is only a nod. You had forgotten what it was like to be unremarkable. It is a mercy, and you take it.

choices.text: Enjoy the stillness

effects.log: It is a long stillness. You use it well.

choices.text: Go looking for a new doctrine

effects.log: You look. It is slow work, and it is your own.

events.text: The first teachers of your school come to you in the evening with a draft of the creed. It is short, plain, and a little frightening in its clarity. It asks something real of whoever swears it, and gives something real back. They have written it on a board hung above the hearth. The board is oak and the ink is fresh. They wait to see whether you will put your name to it.

choices.text: Swear the creed, and sign the board

effects.log: You sign. The ink dries slowly, and the creed settles in you like a seed in damp ground.

choices.text: Decline to sign, but promise to read it daily

effects.log: You promise to read it. The teachers nod. It is not nothing.

events.text: A year after the founding, the creed of your school is read aloud in the yard at the turn of the season. It is short, and everyone knows it by heart, but the reading is the thing. When the last line is spoken, the teachers turn and look at you. It is understood that swearing is for those who mean it. A breeze lifts the corner of the banner. The yard holds its breath.

choices.text: Swear it before the whole school

effects.log: You swear. The yard exhales, and the banner settles.

choices.text: Say you will watch, and learn what it asks

effects.log: The yard murmurs. The teachers accept it, with an air of reserved patience.

events.text: A pupil of your school asks, shyly, if you keep the creed yourself. You hadn't thought of it that way. The creed hangs in the hall, carved in oak, and you walk past it every day. The question hangs in the air like smoke. The pupil does not flinch. It is a child's question, which is to say it is the only real question.

choices.text: Answer by swearing it, then and there

effects.log: You swear, in the corridor, with the pupil as witness. They look relieved and a little awed.

choices.text: Tell the pupil you are still deciding

effects.log: The pupil nods gravely. They will remember this, and so will you.

events.text: A trial of your school's creed is set in the practice yard at dawn. The senior teacher stands at the far end, sword sheathed, and does not move. The creed says that whoever holds it must be able to hold it against a hard hand. The yard is empty but for the two of you and a ring of attentive pupils sitting on the wall. Dew soaks the stones.

choices.text: Hold the creed against the senior teacher

ok.log: You hold. The teacher gives a short bow, and the wall of pupils breathes out as one.

fail.log: The teacher's hand is harder than you thought. You are shown the creed again, patiently, after.

choices.text: Ask to be tested in a later season

effects.log: The teacher says the creed is patient. So is the yard.

events.text: On a damp evening your school puts you to the proof. A stranger, one of the school's old graduates, has come back to test the creed on you. They stand across the table with an easy smile and a very serious pair of hands. The lantern gutters. You are told that anyone who swears the creed can expect this, and that it is not personal.

choices.text: Meet the graduate on their own terms

ok.log: It is a long, honest bout. At the end the graduate laughs, bows, and refills your cup.

fail.log: The graduate wins without cruelty. They help you up and pour the tea themselves.

choices.text: Excuse yourself, and ask to be tested at the new moon

effects.log: The graduate waves a hand. The lantern steadies. There is no hurry.

events.text: The test of your creed is a quiet one. A single closed door in the lower hall, and a note on it: go in. Inside is a bare room and a bench, and on the bench a wooden sword. A voice from nowhere tells you to stand. The sword is the creed. You are not told what to do with it, only to pass the test, and the door shuts behind you with a small, final click.

choices.text: Take up the sword and stand

ok.log: You take it up. The room brightens, the door opens, and the voice says, simply: good.

fail.log: You take it up. The room darkens. The door opens on a corridor of surprised faces.

choices.text: Leave the sword on the bench and wait

effects.log: You wait. After a long time the door opens on its own. Nobody says a word.

events.text: A rich visitor comes to your school with an offer the creed forbids. The visitor is courteous and has brought a gift of silver wrapped in blue silk. The creed says no. The silk says yes. The visitor sets the gift on the table between you and says there is no hurry, in the tone of one who has already made up your mind. The silver catches the lamp.

choices.text: Take the silver, and break the creed

effects.log: You take it. It is a lot of silver. Something in the hall goes quiet.

choices.text: Push the silver back across the table

effects.log: You push it back. The visitor shrugs, and rewraps the silk with a sigh.

events.text: A pupil in difficulty asks you to bend the creed of your school, just a little, just once. The request is sincere and the need is real. You can see exactly how bending would help. You can see, equally, how it would spread. The pupil stands in the doorway with their hands behind their back and looks at the floor.

choices.text: Bend it, once, for the pupil

effects.log: You bend it. The pupil weeps with relief. The creed in the hall seems, faintly, to dim.

choices.text: Hold the creed, and help in another way

effects.log: You hold it. The other way is longer and harder. The pupil thanks you, in time.

events.text: A night of heavy rain, and the creed of your school begins to seem like a rule written by someone who never needed to break it. You sit at the hearth and turn it over. A small voice, your own, says that a creed that cannot flex is a creed that cannot live. The fire pops. The rain is steady. The voice is very reasonable.

choices.text: Listen to the voice, and break the creed

effects.log: You break it, quietly, in the small hours. The rain keeps falling.

choices.text: Banish the voice, and hold to the creed

effects.log: You hold. The fire burns lower. By dawn the voice has gone.

events.text: {npc}, an old guardian of your school's creed, arrives at your gate in the rain. {He} wears no badge and carries a staff. The creed is broken, {he} says, and the school has never forgotten a breach. {He} sets the staff against the wall, takes off a wet hat, and says that you may answer in whichever way you choose.

choices.text: Meet {npc} in the yard

ok.log: The yard rings in the wet. {npc} yields at last, and takes up the staff and the hat.

fail.log: The yard is slick. {npc} wins with a quiet grace, and picks up the hat from the mud.

choices.text: Atone, and hear {npc} out

effects.log: You atone. {npc} listens to all of it, standing in the rain.

events.text: A keeper of the creed, {npc}, comes up the lane from the lower road, thin and weather-beaten, with a walking-stick. {He} stops at your door and says the school has a long memory and a short temper for broken things. {He} does not ask to come in. {He} simply stands there, and waits for you to choose a way to settle the matter.

choices.text: Settle it with the stick and sword

ok.log: It is a lively, noisy settling. {npc} concedes with a tired smile.

fail.log: It is a lively, noisy settling. {npc} wins, and apologises for the bruises.

choices.text: Settle it with words and a penance

effects.log: You offer words and a penance. {npc} accepts them with a nod.

events.text: {npc} has been following you for three days. Tonight {he} sits across the fire in a roadside inn, quiet and entirely unhurried, and says {he} comes from your school. The creed was broken, {he} says, and there is no shame in saying so. {He} will take your account, or {he} will take the matter by force, whichever you prefer. The inn is empty but for the two of you.

choices.text: Choose force, and fight {npc}

ok.log: The inn survives, mostly. {npc} yields, and pays for the broken stool.

fail.log: The inn does not survive well. {npc} wins, and pays for the stool anyway.

choices.text: Choose the account, and speak plainly

effects.log: You speak. {npc} writes it down in a small neat hand.

events.text: The last guardian of the creed leaves your door, and a note is posted at the school gate: the matter is closed. Nobody says whether you were forgiven or merely outlasted. The creed in the hall hangs where it always did. For the first time in years you walk past it without a flinch, and it doesn't seem to mind. A pupil sweeps the steps and does not look up.

choices.text: Pin the note up in your own room

effects.log: It hangs by your bed. Some nights it is a comfort, some nights a reproach.

choices.text: Fold the note and give it to the pupil sweeping

effects.log: The pupil reads it, shrugs, and tucks it into a pocket. They will keep it a very long time.

events.text: It is over. No more guardians come, and the creed no longer hums in your head. The school goes on, and you go on with it. A teacher passing in the corridor nods to you, and it is only a nod. You had forgotten what it was to be unwatched. It is a gift, and you accept it with a hand that is not quite steady.

choices.text: Enjoy the quiet

effects.log: It is a long, plain quiet. You spend it well.

choices.text: Write a new creed of your own

effects.log: You write one, slowly, over several weeks. It is shorter than the old.

events.text: The vow of {phl4_order} is sung, not sworn. At the turn of the season the faction gathers on a floating dais and a cantor leads a line the whole assembly echoes back, rank by rank, voice by voice. Your turn comes between a stout elder and a child. The song is old, and wants a fresh voice. You are given the hush before the first note.

choices.text: Sing the line in your own voice

effects.log: The line goes out over the clouds, and comes back changed, and is yours.

choices.text: Stay silent, hands folded, and let the line pass

effects.log: The dais hums on without you. Nobody pauses, which is also a kindness.

events.text: A seal-carver of {phl4_order} offers to cut you a stamp of the creed, in jade or in plain stone. Whichever you choose, you will press it to your sleeve each morning, and be held to what it says. He lays out both blanks on a cloth, polishes them with the cuff of his sleeve, and looks away so that you may decide without being watched.

choices.text: Choose the plain stone

effects.log: He cuts it that evening. It is warmer than jade, and a little crooked.

choices.text: Push the blanks back across the cloth

effects.log: He wraps them again without comment. The cloth smells of lamp-oil and patience.

events.text: An ancient member of {phl4_order} is dying, and asks for a successor to the creed. Not to the office, only the words. She cannot speak above a whisper. The faction crowds the doorway. She looks past all of them and says your name, and the room turns, and for once nobody is smiling. A cup of water sits by her hand.

choices.text: Kneel, and take the words from her

effects.log: She speaks them. You keep them. The faction watches you rise, changed.

choices.text: Tell her gently that you cannot promise it

effects.log: She smiles, tired and unsurprised. "Then say so to the others," she whispers.

events.text: The faction of {phl4_order} offers the creed in writing, at a long low desk beside the tea-room, no ceremony, no witnesses but a clerk. You may sign in the margin or leave the page blank. The clerk goes on grinding ink and does not look up. It is an almost insulting level of ease for a thing that will govern you for centuries.

choices.text: Sign in the margin

effects.log: The ink dries fast. The clerk blots it with a clean cloth and says, to the cloth, "welcome".

choices.text: Leave the page blank, and take tea instead

effects.log: The clerk pours. The page stays blank. Both of you pretend that is a choice.

events.text: At dawn on the faction's founding day, {phl4_order} sets a bowl of rice on every threshold, and each member eats one grain and pledges aloud. You have been given your bowl. The neighbours' bowls are being emptied one by one, in a murmur that sounds like rain. Yours is full, and the grains sit in it like a small white field.

choices.text: Eat the grain and pledge

effects.log: It tastes of nothing but warmth. The pledge goes out on your breath.

choices.text: Set the bowl back on the step, untouched

effects.log: A sparrow finds it by noon. You consider this a sort of answer.

events.text: The trial of {phl4_order} begins with a bridge: a single plank over a gap in the Isles, with a bell hung at the far end. You must ring it without letting the plank dip. Two seniors watch from the rail. The creed, they say, is held in the soles of the feet before it is held in the head. The wind picks up.

choices.text: Cross the plank with the creed in your stance

ok.log: The plank does not dip. The bell rings once, clear, and the seniors bow together.

fail.log: The plank dips at the middle, and you cling on. The seniors fetch you in, kindly, and send you for tea.

choices.text: Study the plank from the rail, and come back another day

effects.log: The seniors nod. The plank will wait; it has waited longer for others.

events.text: The creed of {phl4_order} is tested in a cold garden at midnight. A senior sits motionless on a stone. You are to take the stone without a word of request, only by the correctness of your bearing. The senior will resist as honestly as honour allows. The frost sparkles, and the garden holds its breath along with you.

choices.text: Take the stone by bearing alone

ok.log: The senior rises slowly, as if lifted by a thread. The stone is yours, and so is the silence.

fail.log: The senior does not move, and you do not either, until the frost turns your hands white. You are led indoors.

choices.text: Bow, and ask for a warmer season

effects.log: The senior inclines their head. "The creed has many seasons," they say.

events.text: Three questions set by an examiner of {phl4_order}, to be answered with a staff in hand: each answer is a form, each form a test of whether the creed has gone into the body. The examiner is perfectly gentle. Between questions they pour tea and speak of the weather. Then they ask the first question, and the staff is a little heavier than before.

choices.text: Answer all three in forms

ok.log: The third form leaves the staff humming. The examiner sets down their cup and says, "Yes."

fail.log: The second form wavers and the third never comes. The examiner pours more tea, without reproach.

choices.text: Ask to answer in words instead

effects.log: The examiner considers this for some time, and allows it for the first question only.

events.text: {phl4_order} sends you to guard a gate for a night, and the trial is that you must let no one pass who cannot give the creed. Hours go by. Then a tall figure in a travelling hat comes up the path, hums, and tries to walk through. They are very polite about it. They are also, you notice, quite strong.

choices.text: Stop the traveller at the gate

ok.log: They stop, laugh, and recite the creed with a grin. They were the examiner all along.

fail.log: They pass you as if through mist, and recite it from the far side, kindly. You will try again.

choices.text: Let them pass, and tell the faction honestly

effects.log: The faction thanks you for your honesty, and writes it in a small, careful book.

events.text: In the rain, in the courtyard of {phl4_order}, two juniors beg a senior for the creed's blessing. The senior says the creed is a burden, not a blessing, and sets a test: a single bowl of water, carried across the courtyard, with the juniors trying to knock it from your hands by any honest means. The rain keeps falling into the bowl.

choices.text: Carry the bowl through the juniors

ok.log: You cross the yard without spilling, though not without laughing. The senior's smile is a long time coming.

fail.log: A junior's elbow gets it in the end, and the bowl goes over. All three of you stand in the puddle.

choices.text: Offer the bowl to the juniors and watch them try

effects.log: They carry it badly and learn something. The senior says nothing, which is high praise.

events.text: A silent contest: you and a member of {phl4_order} sit opposite one another and hold a single cup of water at arm's length. The first to spill, loses. It is the faction's oldest trial, devised, a senior says wryly, by someone with a grudge against wrists. The sun climbs. The cups do not move.

choices.text: Hold the cup past the other's shaking

ok.log: The other spills first, with a small groan of respect. You set yours down very carefully.

fail.log: Your arm trembles at noon, and the water slops. The other takes pity and pours you tea.

choices.text: Offer to share the cup between you

effects.log: The faction has not seen that before. The senior writes it down, thoughtfully.

events.text: A trial of {phl4_order} is held at night on a ledge of the Isles with no rail. A master of the creed stands at the edge and asks you to walk past them to the far lamp. They will not strike. They will only lean. The ledge is narrow, the cloud below is white and endless, and you are quietly aware of every breath.

choices.text: Walk past the leaning master

ok.log: You reach the far lamp. The master straightens and bows, and the cloud below seems less hungry.

fail.log: The lean pushes you back a step, and another, until the lamp is a point of gold you cannot reach. The master leads you in.

choices.text: Step back from the ledge, and ask for a ground-floor test

effects.log: The master smiles. "A reasonable creed has a reasonable floor," they say.

events.text: The creed of {phl4_order} asks you to bring any disputes to the faction's tea-room. A rival has found a quicker way. She offers to settle your grievance in an afternoon, outside the faction, at the cost of a small, quiet exemption. She smiles with all her teeth, and pours your cup first, which is its own kind of hospitality.

choices.text: Take her offer, and let the faction hear later

effects.log: It is settled by supper. The faction hears by morning, and says nothing.

choices.text: Bring the dispute to the tea-room as the creed asks

effects.log: It takes three weeks. The result is slower and holds better.

events.text: Someone at {phl4_order} is quietly selling exemptions: a line in a ledger, a sealed slip, and the vow is lifted for a day. The seller is a friend. They put a slip into your hand and say it is a gift. You can read the date. It is tomorrow, and there is something tomorrow you very badly would like to do.

choices.text: Use the slip

effects.log: You use it. The day is good. The day after, a thin ache starts that does not go.

choices.text: Hand the slip back, and ask them to stop

effects.log: They tear it in half, shamed and relieved. You walk home with a clear conscience and a difficult day ahead.

events.text: An old companion arrives from the lower Isles with a favour to ask, and the favour sits squarely in the gap between what you owe them and what the creed of {phl4_order} allows. They do not argue the point. They sit, dusty from the road, and mention that no one else has ever stood by them.

choices.text: Help them, against the creed

effects.log: You help. They weep with gratitude. You carry the weight of it for years.

choices.text: Help them within the creed, which is less than they wanted

effects.log: They are disappointed, then reconciled. The friendship bends but holds.

events.text: A letter from {phl4_order} praises your devotion to the creed, and names you for an honour reserved for those who have never wavered. You have wavered. The faction does not know. The ceremony is in a week. A pupil has made you a new sash for it. It is very well sewn, and very bright.

choices.text: Say nothing, and accept the honour

effects.log: The honour is yours. The sash feels slightly too tight for years.

choices.text: Write to the faction and confess your lapse before the day

effects.log: The honour is withdrawn. The sash is given to someone else. You sleep well.

events.text: A fine night, a good wine, and an invitation: a rival house of the Isles is throwing a feast, and attendance would mean sitting beside an enemy of {phl4_order} and sharing his bread. The creed does not forbid it in so many words. It forbids it in spirit, which is a worse thing to argue with. Your host is charming.

choices.text: Attend, and eat the bread

effects.log: The bread is good. The enemy turns out to be good company, which makes it worse.

choices.text: Send regrets, and eat at home

effects.log: The regrets are accepted with a pleasant note. Supper at home is cold rice and quiet.

events.text: A student of {phl4_order} shows you a shortcut around a point of the creed. It is clever. It has been used by half the faction for years. Nobody calls it a breach; they call it a custom. You can see exactly why it works, and exactly what it costs, and the student is waiting, eager and a little afraid, to learn which you will call it.

choices.text: Use the custom, as the others do

effects.log: It works, and keeps working. You stop noticing the cost after the first year.

choices.text: Name it a breach, and decline to use it

effects.log: The student goes quiet. Some of the faction stops speaking to you. Some start.

events.text: On a night of spring thaw a stranger with a cloud-lantern presents a bargain. The creed of {phl4_order} has bound your hands for decades, he says, and what has it given? He lists the things you did not do. His list is long and exact. He holds out an alternative with nothing written on it at all.

choices.text: Take the blank page

effects.log: The page is light. For a time you do not miss the creed, and then you do.

choices.text: Show him your own list of what the creed gave

effects.log: Your list is shorter, and denser. He folds his own, and bows.

events.text: {npc}, a hunter of {phl4_order}, has reached your isle by the evening ferry. {He} brings no weapon, only a lacquered box. The box holds the creed you broke, {he} says, in the form it took the day you broke it. {He} will open it only if you agree to hear what is inside. The ferrywoman lingers on the dock, curious.

choices.text: Refuse the box, and fight {npc} on the landing

ok.log: The landing creaks and holds. {npc} bows and leaves the box unopened on the planks.

fail.log: The landing gives way under both of you, to the delight of the ferrywoman. {npc} drags you out by the collar.

choices.text: Open the box, and hear what is inside

effects.log: It is a single sheet of paper with your own handwriting on it. You read it all.

events.text: A hunter of {phl4_order} is waiting at your door when you wake, {npc}, calm and slightly damp. {He} has been standing in the dew since dawn. The creed requires a witness to every breach, {he} says, and the witness is {him}. {He} will speak for the faction or for you, depending on what is done today. There is no unkindness in {his} voice.

choices.text: Defy the witness, and meet {npc} in the garden

ok.log: You win by a hand's breadth. {npc} nods like a person confirming a suspicion.

fail.log: You lose by a hand's breadth, and {npc} bows before helping you up.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to speak for you

effects.log: {npc} speaks. It is a more accurate account than you could have given, and harder to hear.

events.text: A boy of the Isles delivers a message: {npc}, hunter of {phl4_order}, is waiting at the teahouse on the south pier. {He} has ordered for two. The boy says this twice, wide-eyed, before running off. The teahouse has been emptied of other patrons. Two cups, steaming, sit across the table from each other.

choices.text: Refuse to sit, and meet {npc} on the pier

ok.log: The pier shakes. {npc} yields, with a sigh, and pays for both cups.

fail.log: The pier shakes. {npc} wins, and you both go to drink the tea afterwards, slightly awkwardly.

choices.text: Sit, and drink, and answer

effects.log: The tea cools while you talk. {npc} writes it all down, carefully, and thanks you for the cup.

events.text: The wind brings {npc} to you in a gust, a hunter of {phl4_order} in a travelling cloak with a single reed whistle hanging at {his} chest. {He} blows it once. Every bird on the isle falls silent. The creed was broken, {he} says. Not a threat, a fact, and {he} would like to settle it under the open sky, one way or the other.

choices.text: Answer the whistle with a challenge

ok.log: Birds and wind settle. {npc} lowers the whistle, grudging and satisfied.

fail.log: The whistle is louder than you thought. When it stops, you are sitting down and {npc} is offering a hand.

choices.text: Answer the whistle with an apology

effects.log: {npc} puts the whistle away. The birds begin again, a few at a time.

events.text: At the end of a long cloud-road you find {npc} sitting on a milestone, a hunter of {phl4_order}, eating a pear. {He} offers you half. The breach, {he} says, was seen from a distance, and weighed at leisure, and {he} would like to know whether you meant it. It is an oddly gentle question, and the pear is good.

choices.text: Decline the pear and the question, and fight

ok.log: The milestone is cracked in half. {npc} wipes pear off {his} chin and concedes.

fail.log: The milestone survives. You do not. {npc} finishes the pear.

choices.text: Eat the pear, and tell {him} whether you meant it

effects.log: You tell {him}. The pear is gone before you finish talking.

events.text: The faction of {phl4_order} sends one final note, brief and formal: the account is closed and your name struck from the ledger of breaches. A courier carries it up the White Stairs in a lacquered tube. You read it on the landing, in front of the courier, who says nothing. When you finish, the courier asks, very quietly, if you would like a cup of tea.

choices.text: Accept the tea, and sit on the landing a while

effects.log: You sit. The courier talks about the weather. It is the best conversation you have had in weeks.

choices.text: Pay the courier, and take the note inside

effects.log: You read it again, alone. It does not change, and neither do you.

events.text: The last hunter of {phl4_order} has gone home. You notice it first at breakfast, when the sound you had been bracing against is simply absent. Your cook sets down an egg, then another, as if she, too, has been waiting for you to put on weight. The creed still hangs in the room, but it is no longer pointed at you.

choices.text: Spend the morning in the garden, doing nothing

effects.log: The garden does not mind. You feel, quite suddenly, young.

choices.text: Go find the creed's oldest scroll and read it anew

effects.log: It reads differently now. It is shorter than you remembered.

events.text: The doctrine of {phl4_order} is offered at the midwinter feast, between the fish and the sweet. A priest carries a tray of small clay tokens, each stamped with the doctrine's mark, among the gods at table. Taking one is swearing. Passing the tray on is not an insult. The tray reaches you. Everyone at your end of the table is suddenly very interested in their rice.

choices.text: Take a token, and close your hand over it

effects.log: The clay is warm. The priest moves on without ceremony, and the table exhales.

choices.text: Pass the tray along with a nod

effects.log: The tray goes on down the table. Nobody says anything, and the fish is very good.

events.text: A choir of {phl4_order} sings the doctrine at dawn on the steps of its mother temple, and any god who joins the last verse is counted as sworn. You arrive late, and stand at the back, with your mouth open, and find you know the tune. The last verse comes. The choirmaster looks directly at you.

choices.text: Sing the last verse with them

effects.log: Your voice carries. The choirmaster inclines her head, and the verse closes on a held note.

choices.text: Close your mouth and stay at the back

effects.log: The verse ends without you. A child in the choir stares at you as if you had stolen something.

events.text: The doctrine of {phl4_order} is inscribed on a bronze bell, and a god takes the vow by striking the bell once and listening to the note. You are brought before it. The bell is cold, enormous and green with age. A mallet hangs beside it on a thong. The priests stand back, as if the bell might be insulted by observation.

choices.text: Strike the bell

effects.log: The note goes out over the domains. It stays in you for a long time after.

choices.text: Lay a palm on the bell without striking

effects.log: It hums against your hand, faintly. You step back, and nobody objects.

events.text: A high priest of {phl4_order} comes to your temple with a scroll sealed in blue wax, and says the doctrine will not be forced, only offered, and then he stands in your doorway for an entire afternoon without moving. Your own priests circle him nervously. By evening the whole temple is waiting to see who will outlast whom.

choices.text: Break the seal and read the scroll

effects.log: It is short and plain. You read it twice, and put your name beneath.

choices.text: Offer him a chair and tea, and no answer

effects.log: He drinks the tea and does not press. He leaves the scroll behind, still sealed.

events.text: A mortal worshipper asks you which doctrine to follow, and points to {phl4_order} among several. You find you have no clean answer. The worshipper is old and patient and has brought you an apple. If you vouch for the doctrine, they will follow it; if you do not, they will choose another. They sit down on the step to wait.

choices.text: Vouch for the doctrine, and take the vow yourself

effects.log: You say the vow before the worshipper, and they say it after you. The apple is bruised and sweet.

choices.text: Tell them honestly that you cannot decide for them

effects.log: They nod, bite the apple, and go off to think.

events.text: The trial of {phl4_order} is held in a rice-paddy at dawn, the water ankle-deep, the mud cold, a single plank across. A senior priest stands in the middle of the plank. The doctrine says to pass, not around, not under. The senior holds a long pole and is entirely sincere in being an obstacle. A heron watches the whole thing.

choices.text: Push through the senior on the plank

ok.log: The plank sags, the senior steps aside, and the heron takes off in disgust.

fail.log: You go into the paddy up to the waist. The senior helps you out with the pole and no comment.

choices.text: Wade around and ask for a drier trial

effects.log: The senior suppresses a smile. "Then we shall find one," they say.

events.text: Before the high shrine of {phl4_order}, a god of the trial blocks the path with a torch and a small, hard smile. To pass the shrine, you must show that the doctrine has changed you, with your hands, not your words. The god lowers the torch. The flame leans toward you as if hungry for an answer.

choices.text: Strike the torch aside

ok.log: The flame gutters and flares; the god yields. The shrine door swings wide on its own.

fail.log: The torch flares and singes your sleeve. The god pulls it back, apologetic, and sends you to the cool well.

choices.text: Wait for the flame to settle and try tomorrow

effects.log: The god nods. The doctrine, they say, is patient.

events.text: On a feast-day of {phl4_order}, the festival crowd parts to reveal a ring of sand with a dozen priests seated around it. In the ring stands a young god with a staff. You are to cross the ring without being touched by the staff. The crowd murmurs. Someone has already begun taking odds on the outcome, in whispers.

choices.text: Dodge through the staff's sweep

ok.log: You cross with a hand's breadth to spare. The crowd roars, and the young god salutes.

fail.log: The staff taps your shin lightly. You hop out, laughing, to a round of applause.

choices.text: Bow out of the ring, and thank the crowd

effects.log: The crowd is kind. The young god bows back, and the sand is raked smooth.

events.text: {phl4_order} sets you a trial in an empty courtyard with only a bowl of water and a flute. The bowl must be moved from one side to the other. The flute must be played while you do it. The master listens from a balcony, and stirs his tea in rhythm to what you play. You are not told what the score is.

choices.text: Carry the bowl across, playing steadily

ok.log: The bowl crosses without spilling a drop. The tune lasts exactly as long as the walk.

fail.log: The tune falters in the middle and the bowl slops. The master smiles and sets down his tea.

choices.text: Play first and carry after, in two trials

effects.log: The master laughs, softly. "Honest," he says. "Come back when you can do both."

events.text: A test of {phl4_order}: you must defend a single lit candle from a sequence of acolytes, each bearing a fan. They approach one by one, cheerfully, intent on putting it out. The candle is the doctrine, a senior explains, and the fans are the world. The acolytes are young and enthusiastic, and clearly well fed.

choices.text: Shield the flame through all the fans

ok.log: The last acolyte fans, and the flame leans, and holds. The acolytes cheer despite themselves.

fail.log: The sixth fan does it. The candle sulks, and the acolytes are very sorry.

choices.text: Cup the flame, and ask them to wait for a calmer hour

effects.log: They agree, grumbling. The candle burns in a niche until the winds drop.

events.text: A test by the elders of {phl4_order} in the cold dawn at the edge of the lower heavens: climb a stair of nine hundred steps while three elders recite the doctrine in counterpoint, each at a different speed. You must keep your own pace and your own count, or else fall back to the first step.

choices.text: Climb through the counterpoint without losing count

ok.log: At the top you are shaking, and the elders applaud, three claps out of time with each other.

fail.log: You lose count at six hundred and start over. The elders continue to recite, serenely, as you descend.

choices.text: Ask for the stair to be shortened, or the elders silenced

effects.log: The elders confer, and silence two of them. It takes you only half the morning.

events.text: Late one evening, a high god of the doctrine of {phl4_order} turns up at your gate with a basket of apples, as if on a social call. She offers one. It is cold in the hand, and when you bite, you realise the apple is the trial: she is testing whether the doctrine will let you take what you want, or only what is given. She waits, smiling.

choices.text: Fight her for the whole basket

ok.log: You grab the basket. She laughs, hands you another, and says that was an acceptable answer.

fail.log: She keeps the basket, and your arm. She releases both, apologising, in good time.

choices.text: Eat the one you were given and thank her

effects.log: She eats an apple beside you. The basket stays shut.

events.text: A temple of a rival pantheon sends you a gift: a statue of your own likeness, in gold. The doctrine of {phl4_order} says no tribute from rivals. The statue is very good. Your priests are weeping with delight. A card tucked beneath the base says only: we admire your work. The statue's eyes follow you around the room.

choices.text: Accept the statue and set it in the court

effects.log: It stands in your court for centuries. The doctrine never quite looks at it.

choices.text: Send it back with a letter of thanks

effects.log: The rival temple is disappointed and impressed in equal measure.

events.text: The doctrine of {phl4_order} forbids the use of a god's name in an oath, and tonight a mortal worshipper begs you to swear by yours on a matter of life or death. Not hers. A neighbour's. She will not believe you otherwise. The words would be easy. She kneels in the dust with a face of pure appeal.

choices.text: Swear by your name, as asked

effects.log: The oath is taken. It is believed, and kept, and the doctrine goes slightly cold in your hand.

choices.text: Refuse the oath, and offer your help without it

effects.log: She is confused, then moved. The help is real, and she is wary and grateful.

events.text: A scribe of the Heavenly Court offers you a quiet loophole: a sentence in the Book of Fates that, correctly cited, lets a god skip one clause of {phl4_order}. He has done it for others. He wants nothing but the satisfaction of having been of service. His quill is poised over the page like a patient insect.

choices.text: Let him cite it

effects.log: He writes. The clause vanishes. The doctrine hangs in the air, slightly thinner.

choices.text: Have him strike the sentence instead

effects.log: He grumbles, but complies. The Book of Fates is a little tidier.

events.text: A great festival is on, and every god in the domain is dancing in the temple court. The doctrine of {phl4_order} bids you refrain from public revels, and the revels are splendid. A god of wine pulls at your sleeve and says nobody will tell. Your own priests are clapping time, and glancing at you with something like hope.

choices.text: Dance, with abandon

effects.log: You dance. It is wonderful, and you wake with the rhythm still in your feet and a faint tightness around the doctrine.

choices.text: Watch from the colonnade, clapping lightly

effects.log: The colonnade is cool. The revels go on without you, and nothing is lost but a story.

events.text: A starving village prays to you for grain, and the doctrine of {phl4_order} says a god must not meddle in the harvests of another's field. The granary of a nearby god sits full and idle. A boy at your altar offers his only coin. You could, with a few words, send a little across.

choices.text: Move the grain, and bear the breach

effects.log: The village eats. The neighbouring god never misses it, and the doctrine marks you down.

choices.text: Ask the neighbouring god politely for a loan

effects.log: The god is amused, and slow, and kind. The grain arrives a week late.

events.text: A scroll arrives from a former pupil of {phl4_order} who left the doctrine long ago. She is now prosperous and cheerful, and she has written a seven-page account of how she did it. The last page lists the things she no longer has to do. It reads, God help you, like an advertisement. Her seal is a smiling fish.

choices.text: Follow her example, one step at a time

effects.log: The first step is easy. The second is easier. By the tenth you have forgotten what you were leaving.

choices.text: Reply with thanks, and a list of what she gave up

effects.log: Her answer is long, and slightly shaken. You do not reply again.

events.text: Your priests have found a way to double the offerings of your temple, by a trick of the ledger the doctrine of {phl4_order} would disapprove of. Nothing is stolen. Nothing is lied about, exactly. Worshippers would be a little poorer and a little happier. The temple treasurer lays the scheme out for you, sweating, on a sheet of rice-paper.

choices.text: Approve the scheme

effects.log: The offerings double. The doctrine feels like a coat that no longer quite fits.

choices.text: Burn the paper, and keep the old ledger

effects.log: The treasurer wipes his forehead and says nothing. Offerings stay as they were.

events.text: {npc}, an inquisitor of {phl4_order}, climbs the steps of your temple in a plain brown robe and bare feet, carrying a scale. {He} sets it down on your altar and balances a feather on one pan. You broke the doctrine, {he} says, and the scale will find the weight of it, if you permit. {He} bows. The scale does not.

choices.text: Refuse the scale, and fight {npc} on the steps

ok.log: The scale tips over. {npc} yields, with reluctant dignity, and picks it up.

fail.log: The scale holds steady. {npc} wins with a mild expression, and rights it.

choices.text: Allow the scale, and answer for the breach

effects.log: The feather and the weight come level. {npc} writes the result down.

events.text: A hunter of {phl4_order} is waiting in your shrine when you return from the evening rite, kneeling in front of your altar with a bowl of rice. {npc} has been there since noon. Your priests did not dare to disturb {him}. {He} says the doctrine was broken, that {he} is sorry to be the one, and that the rice is, in fact, an offering.

choices.text: Strike the bowl from {his} hands

ok.log: The rice scatters like a blessing. {npc} bows, once, and yields.

fail.log: The bowl stays. {npc} catches your wrist very gently, and holds it until you stop.

choices.text: Kneel beside {him} and eat the rice

effects.log: You eat. {npc} writes down everything you say, between mouthfuls.

events.text: {npc} arrives at the Gate of Offerings in the rain, dripping, one of {phl4_order}'s grimmest hunters, and says nothing at all. {He} stands there until the gate-keeper brings an umbrella, and then stands under that. The breach was grave. {He} has no need to say so. The rain drums on the umbrella like a slow, mournful drum.

choices.text: Meet {npc} at the gate, and settle it

ok.log: The rain lessens, as if pleased. {npc} lowers {his} head in surrender.

fail.log: The rain gets heavier. {npc} wins quietly and holds the umbrella over you after.

choices.text: Invite {npc} in and answer the breach

effects.log: You tell all of it by the lamp. {npc} listens, and drips on the matting.

events.text: A hunter of {phl4_order}, {npc}, has found you in the market of the divine exchange, haggling over incense. {He} stands at your elbow and orders a cup of plum tea. When it arrives {he} sets it down between you and says: when you are done with the incense, we should talk about the doctrine. It is not a request, but it is not unfriendly.

choices.text: Finish the haggling and challenge {npc} on the spot

ok.log: The market parts around you like a school of fish. {npc} bows out, and pays for the incense.

fail.log: The market parts around you. {npc} wins, and buys you the incense anyway.

choices.text: Finish your tea, and your confession, together

effects.log: {npc} takes notes on the back of a receipt. It is not unlike a friendly chat.

events.text: {npc} stands in the empty central hall of your temple at midnight, an inquisitor of {phl4_order} with a lantern held low. The lantern is not for light but for show. The doctrine, {he} says, has a memory like a river, and the breach left a stain. {He} has come to wash it, one way or another.

choices.text: Dash the lantern and fight in the dark

ok.log: The hall goes black. When the lamps are relit, {npc} is on one knee, conceding.

fail.log: The hall goes black. When the lamps are relit, you are on one knee, and {npc} is offering a hand.

choices.text: Take the lantern from {him}, and say it all aloud

effects.log: You speak into the lamp's small circle. {npc} listens, and the stain lightens.

events.text: The doctrine of {phl4_order} issues a quiet decree: your breach is forgiven and the file closed. The notice is pinned to the temple gate by a young priest who looks relieved to be rid of it. Worshippers read it as they pass, and look at you, and then, politely, away. A child asks her mother what 'forgiven' means.

choices.text: Read the notice, and take it down yourself

effects.log: The paper is stiff. You fold it small and tuck it in a sleeve.

choices.text: Leave it for the rain to take

effects.log: By the second storm it is a pulp on the step. You sweep it away and feel unburdened.

events.text: A last visit from {phl4_order}: a lay brother with a sack of dried apricots and an envelope. Inside, the doctrine's decision, in three lines. He apologises for the apricots, which he was told to bring, and does not know why. You eat one on the doorstep. They are sweet and sticky, and the sack is easily big enough for the temple.

choices.text: Share the apricots with the temple

effects.log: The priests are delighted. The doctrine's decision is read aloud over a feast.

choices.text: Eat them alone, over a quiet evening

effects.log: The evening is soft. You do not think about the doctrine once.

events.text: At the feast of the school's founding, every pupil and teacher of your school writes the creed on a strip of paper and feeds it to the bonfire. Tonight it is your turn. The paper is blank, a stub of charcoal beside it. The senior teacher looks into the fire and does not watch you. The younger pupils watch very closely indeed.

choices.text: Write the creed in your own hand, and feed it to the fire

effects.log: The paper curls, and for a moment the flame is a clear gold.

choices.text: Hand the blank strip to the fire

effects.log: The fire takes it. Nobody remarks. A pupil behind you coughs.

events.text: The creed of your school is carved on a door-post of the front gate, and everyone who comes in touches it with a thumb. For years you have passed it by, thinking of other things. Today a teacher blocks the way and asks, mildly, whether you ever read it. You haven't. She waits while you do.

choices.text: Read it through, and press your thumb to the last line

effects.log: The wood is polished by ten thousand thumbs. Yours fits among them.

choices.text: Say it is not yours to read yet

effects.log: The teacher steps aside. The carving stays as it was, blunt and patient.

events.text: A wandering poet comes to your school and asks to be shown the creed. When he is shown, he reads it, laughs, and says it would look better as a song. He sings it, wrong, in a grating voice, and the pupils are scandalised and then wiping their eyes. He bows to you and asks if you would sing it right.

choices.text: Sing it as it should be sung

effects.log: Your voice cracks on the high note, and the hall holds it anyway.

choices.text: Laugh with the others, and let it go unsung

effects.log: The poet shrugs, pockets his lute, and is gone by morning.

events.text: A trial of your school's creed is called in the orchard, among the plum trees, with no warning. A senior pupil with a bamboo pole stands in the path and asks you to pass without bruising the fruit. Neither can be struck. The pole is long, the plums are ripe, and the grass is slick with dew. The branches rustle.

choices.text: Slip past the pole without touching a plum

ok.log: You come through with the fruit all intact. The senior laughs, a short, surprised bark.

fail.log: A plum drops, then another. The senior picks them up and hands them to you, wordless.

choices.text: Ask to try it again after the harvest

effects.log: The senior shrugs. "Fruit isn't going anywhere," they say.

events.text: On a feast evening the elders of your school call you into the courtyard and ask you to defend the creed against three at once, in play. They hold wooden swords. They are old, and quick, and smile as they come. The torches flare in the wind. Your classmates are leaning out of every window.

choices.text: Fend off all three with the creed in your stance

ok.log: You come out of the circle tangled and laughing. The elders bow in order of seniority.

fail.log: The three tap you, shoulder, knee, ear. You count them, and the elders refill your cup.

choices.text: Ask them to come at you one at a time

effects.log: They oblige, after consultation. It takes the whole evening.

events.text: A test of your school's creed is set on the old stone bridge in the rain. A veteran teacher stands in the middle with a lantern and a stout walking-stick and asks you to cross. The bridge is narrow, the river is loud, and the stick is solid. You hold the creed in one hand and your balance in the other.

choices.text: Cross the bridge past the stick

ok.log: You step onto the far bank with the lantern, grinning. The teacher's grumble is almost fond.

fail.log: You slip, and the stick catches you by the belt. Both of you are soaked.

choices.text: Wait for the rain to stop before crossing

effects.log: The teacher sits on the parapet and shares a pipe. The rain stops at midnight.

events.text: A bell rings in the middle of the night at your school, and the creed's trial begins in the dark: you are to find your way across the long hall to the far door, while a teacher listens for your steps. Floorboards creak, curtains hang, the teacher's cup clinks. They are very good at listening.

choices.text: Cross unheard, with the creed in your stride

ok.log: You reach the door. The teacher is still listening when you tap their shoulder.

fail.log: A board creaks at the wrong moment. The teacher lights a candle, and you both laugh.

choices.text: Ask for the lamp to be lit and the trial postponed

effects.log: The teacher lights the lamp. "A fair request," they say. "Try again on a new moon."

events.text: In the cold of the new year your school hosts a gathering of the creed's old graduates, and the youngest of them is chosen to test you: a lean person with a face full of freckles and a sword that has never been drawn in anger. They bow. You bow back. The guests settle on benches to watch, cups in hand.

choices.text: Test the freckled graduate in the swept yard

ok.log: It is a bright, quick exchange. At its end both of you are breathless, and bowing.

fail.log: The graduate is faster than they look. A tap on the ribs ends it, and a cup is pressed into your hand.

choices.text: Excuse yourself from the yard, and promise a rematch

effects.log: The graduate looks relieved, then amused. The rematch takes place the next spring.

events.text: A wealthy merchant visits your school and offers a generous endowment on the condition that you waive one small clause of the creed, just once, for his nephew. The nephew is pleasant, and clearly not up to it. The merchant puts a heavy purse on the table and looks at the rafters. The school's roof, you remember, leaks.

choices.text: Take the purse and waive the clause

effects.log: The roof is mended before winter. The clause sits in the dust.

choices.text: Push the purse back across the table

effects.log: The merchant sighs, collects it, and leaves the nephew a spare coat.

events.text: A pupil you like asks you to look away while they break a rule of the creed to save a friend. Not a large rule. Not a harmful one. The friend is in trouble, and the creed would see them expelled. The pupil's hands are shaking. A single lamp is lit in the corridor, and you are the only one in it.

choices.text: Look away, and say nothing

effects.log: You do. The friend is saved, and so, in a way, is the pupil. The creed does not forget.

choices.text: Help them find a way that keeps the creed

effects.log: It takes two nights and a bag of persuasion. The creed holds and so does the friend.

events.text: A dealer in antiques comes by with a lacquered box, and inside it a scroll said to be the school's first creed, in the founder's hand, authentic and priceless. It differs, he notes, from the one you swore by. He suggests it would be profitable to prefer the older text. He does not say who to. His eyes are very bright.

choices.text: Buy the scroll, and adopt the older text

effects.log: The older text is looser. It is easier to live by, and you notice it.

choices.text: Tell him the school keeps the creed it swore

effects.log: He packs up his box with a half-bow. The scroll leaves with him.

events.text: Lightning takes the old pine at the school's gate, and in the night a neighbour comes asking to cut and sell it. The creed says the pine is not to be touched. The neighbour is poor, the pine is valuable, and the school is empty but for you. The neighbour holds a saw, and does not look at you.

choices.text: Nod, and let them take the pine

effects.log: The saw sings through the night. In the morning there is a stump and a bag of coin.

choices.text: Offer the neighbour work and wages instead

effects.log: It costs you and the school. The pine stays, and the neighbour thanks you gruffly.

events.text: Two pupils bring you a dispute over a copied scroll, and the creed says to refer it to the senior teacher. The senior teacher is away. The pupils are impatient. One of them is, you suspect, lying. A quick decision from you would end it tonight, outside the creed. The two pupils stand in the doorway, shoulder to shoulder, waiting.

choices.text: Settle it yourself, against the creed

effects.log: You settle it. It is a fair settling, and a breach. The senior teacher raises an eyebrow on return.

choices.text: Make them wait for the senior teacher

effects.log: It takes four days. They are both furious and both relieved.

events.text: {npc}, a stern guardian of your school's creed, comes down the road at dusk with a lantern and an old, folded cloak. {He} sets the lantern on the gatepost and says the breach has been counted. Counted by whom, you do not ask. {He} unrolls the cloak and shows you two staves. {He} offers you your pick.

choices.text: Take a stave and meet {npc} in the lane

ok.log: The lane rings with it. At the end {npc} lowers {his} stave and picks up the lantern.

fail.log: The lane rings with it. At the end you are sitting on the gatepost and {npc} is rubbing {his} wrist.

choices.text: Put the staves aside and sit down to account for yourself

effects.log: You talk by the lantern until it burns low. {npc} listens with the cloak on {his} knees.

events.text: A guardian of the creed, {npc}, is sitting at your table when you come home, drinking tea made with your own kettle. {He} did not break in; the neighbours let {him} in. The breach is known, {he} says. {He} would rather settle it before supper than after. The cat is on {his} lap.

choices.text: Refuse the tea, and demand {npc} step outside

ok.log: It is brisk and bright. {npc} concedes, and puts the cat down with great care.

fail.log: It is brisk and bright. {npc} wins, and apologises to the cat.

choices.text: Pour yourself a cup and answer for the breach

effects.log: You answer, over two cups. {npc} says it will do.

events.text: The last letter from your school's creed-keepers arrives with the carrier, thin and unsealed. It says only that the breach is closed, with no signature. The carrier, noticing your face, has the grace to look at the horses. You read it twice, standing in the lane, and fold it into your sleeve like a pressed flower.

choices.text: Pin the letter above your bed

effects.log: It stays there for years, yellowing slowly.

choices.text: Walk to the river and sit there a while

effects.log: The river is brown and unconcerned. It is a good place to be forgiven.
